extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and evaluating definitions and classifications: what counts as a correct/complete definition, types of imperfect definitions, the distinction between definitions of names vs 'definitions of things', and classification of attributes (proprium, accidens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as a proposition declaratory of the meaning of a word
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest and most correct notion of a Definition is, a proposition declaratory of the meaning of a word; namely, either the meaning which it bears in common acceptation, or that which the speaker or writer, for the particular purposes of his discourse, intends to annex to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A definition states the connotation of a term either directly (explicitly declaring the attributes) or indirectly (by predicating other connotative names). It is essentially an explanation of the use/meaning of the sign (word).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names are unsusceptible of definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Words which have no meaning are unsusceptible of definition. Proper names, therefore, can not be defined. A proper name being a mere mark put upon an individual, and of which it is the characteristic property to be destitute of meaning, its meaning can not of course be declared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot define a proper name by listing attributes (e.g., 'John Thomson is the son of General Thomson' is not a definition of the name). You may only point out the individual to indicate the referent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a connotative name is declaration of its connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of connotative names, the meaning ... is the connotation; and the definition of a connotative name, is the proposition which declares its connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct form: state the attributes the name connote. Indirect form: predicate synonymous connotative names or several names that together reproduce the full connotation (e.g., 'Man is a corporeal, organized, animated, rational being, shaped so and so').

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete (philosophical) definition = sum total of essential propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of a name, according to this view of it, is the sum total of all the essential propositions which can be framed with that name for their subject. All propositions the truth of which is implied in the name, ... are included in the definition, if complete, and may be evolved from it without the aid of any other premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete definition is an analysis that resolves the meaning into all constituent attributes; brevity is secondary to exhaustiveness. This is the standard for philosophical/scientific precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining single-attribute (abstract) names by analyzing their foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the abstract name does not express a complication of attributes, but a single attribute, ... the foundation of the attribute (the fact or phenomenon) must be analyzed into parts to obtain a definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., 'Eloquence' (one attribute) is grounded on a phenomenon (power of influencing feelings by speech or writing) which can be dissected into cause and effect to produce a definition. Definitions of attributes proceed from analysis of their experiential foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of simple feelings are practically undefinable
rubrics_metrics.description: The only names which are unsusceptible of definition, because their meaning is unsusceptible of analysis, are the names of the simple feelings themselves. These are in the same condition as proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such terms (e.g., a raw sensation word) cannot be defined verbally; one must appeal directly to the individual's experience (there are no more primitive words to analyze them with).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential but incomplete definitions (practical/ordinary adequacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: An imperfect definition which defines a connotative term by a part only of its connotation, but a part sufficient to mark out correctly the boundaries of its denotation (e.g., 'Man is a rational animal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are acceptable for ordinary use because they sufficiently indicate denotation; however they are incomplete philosophically and may be overturned by discovery of new objects (vulnerability to counterexamples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental definitions (descriptions) are not genuine definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions in which the name of a class is defined by any of its accidents—that is, by attributes which are not included in its connotation—has been rejected from the rank of genuine Definition by all logicians, and has been termed Description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions may nevertheless serve to identify denotation if they are convertible with the term in practice (e.g., 'Man is a featherless biped'); they are classificatory shortcuts, but not analytic definitions tied to the essence of the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition per genus et differentiam (and its limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logicians laid down the rule that the definition of a species should be per genus et differentiam. Differentia is seldom taken to mean the whole of the peculiarities constitutive of the species, but some one of those peculiarities only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A philosophically complete definition would require 'per genus et differentias' (all differentiæ). The rule fails for the highest genus (summum genus) which has no superior genus; hence per genus et differentiam is not universally tenable as a completeness criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific/technical definitions serve classification and are provisional
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific definitions ... have for their object to serve as the landmarks of scientific classification. Since classifications in any science are continually modified as scientific knowledge advances, the definitions in the sciences are also constantly varying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical definitions may assign special connotation to an ordinary term for classificatory purposes (e.g., Cuvier's 'man' as mammiferous animal with two hands). They can be legitimate definitions within a scientific scheme but must be seen as provisional and sensitive to empirical change (acid example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish definitions of names from 'definitions of things' (no factual content)
rubrics_metrics.description: All definitions are of names, and of names only; though in some definitions, besides explaining the meaning of the word, it is intended to be implied that there exists a thing corresponding to the word. The covert assertion of existence is not a definition but a postulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful: a genuine definition states meaning and cannot by itself assert existence or supply factual premises. When a definition appears to assert existence (as in some Euclidean definitions), that element is a separate postulate and should be treated as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat nominal definitions as factual premises without an existence postulate
rubrics_metrics.description: If definitions are used as premises without the tacit assumption of real existence, one may infer only propositions about meanings (words), not about real things. To use a definition to infer facts requires an additional postulate that things with those properties exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Euclid's 'circle' contains both a definitional nominal part and a covert postulate that such a figure may be described. Analysts should substitute 'means' for 'is' to avoid conflating definition with existence. Beware of drawing empirical conclusions from mere definitions (dragon example shows the paradox).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about covert postulates in definitions used for demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Many purported definitions used as premises in demonstrations contain, besides the nominal definition, an implicit assumption (postulate) that objects with the defined properties can exist; demonstrations actually rely on those postulates rather than on the nominal definition itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formal reasoning relies on a definition to construct or assume a figure/object, explicitly state the postulate permitting its existence. Eliminating the hidden postulate does not permit the theorem to stand; therefore separate linguistic definitions from existential assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of attributes: Proprium vs Accidens (and subkinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proprium: any attribute which belongs to all the individuals included in the species, and which ... follows from some attribute which the name either ordinarily or specially connotes. Accidens: attributes which are neither involved in the signification of the name nor have any necessary connection with attributes which are so involved; divided into Separable and Inseparable Accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proprium may follow by demonstration (first kind) or by causation (second kind) — both are necessary consequences. Inseparable accidents are universal but not necessary (blackness of crows presently universal but not connoted); separable accidents are sometimes absent (color of a European, being born at a time). Use these categories to evaluate whether a trait is essential, necessary consequence, or accidental for classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of Proprium: demonstrative and causal necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: One attribute may follow from another in two ways ... It may follow as a conclusion follows premises (demonstration), or it may follow as an effect follows a cause (causation). ... whether a Proprium follows by demonstration or by causation, it follows necessarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging if an attribute is a proprium, determine whether its necessity is inferential (logical/demonstrative) or causal. Example: equal opposite sides in a parallelogram (demonstrable), capacity for language from rationality in man (causal). This distinction informs how definitions and inferences are structured.
